&l;p&g;&l;img class=&q;dam-image shutterstock size-large wp-image-1080176045&q; src=&q;https://specials-images.forbesimg.com/dam/imageserve/1080176045/960×0.jpg?fit=scale&q; data-height=&q;640&q; data-width=&q;960&q;&g; Shutterstock
It&a;rsquo;s hard to talk about financial confidence without also looking at financial knowledge. How can you be confident about something if you don&a;rsquo;t understand it?
This is the chicken/egg conversation at the heart of the relationship between people and money, as demonstrated by two recent surveys looking at how a lack of knowledge/confidence can harm your financial life (though &l;a href=&q;http://www.forbes.com/sites/elizabethharris/2017/06/29/the-confidence-paradox-could-womens-lack-of-investing-confidence-be-an-investing-edge/&q;&g;&l;em&g;overconfidence&l;/em&g;&l;/a&g; can also take a toll on investment performance).
First, there&a;rsquo;s the question of knowledge. According to the findings from the&a;nbsp;&l;a href=&q;http://gflec.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/04/TIAA_GFLEC_Report_PFinIndex_April2018_fin.pdf?x87657&q; target=&q;_blank&q;&g;2018 TIAA Institute-GFLEC Personal Finance Index&l;/a&g;&a;nbsp;report, more men than women, on average, performed better answering questions on eight money subject areas including earning, consuming, saving, investing, borrowing/managing debt, insuring, comprehending risk and recognizing appropriate sources of information and advice.
The results show 21% of men answered 75% of the questions correctly, compared to just 12% of the female survey participants, according to findings released this month. (Though that slim minority in both genders &a;mdash; effectively scoring a &a;ldquo;C&a;rdquo; in financial literacy &a;mdash; is nothing to cheer about.)
The stakes are substantial. According to the survey, participants posting higher scores were more likely to be able to cover an unexpected $2,000 expense, pay monthly bills without incurring overdraft fees and showed a penchant for retirement planning. In other words, three areas that can cause significant stress tend to be avoided more often by those who score higher on financial literacy tests.
For women, there are compelling and unique challenges that suggest we should be spending &l;em&g;even more attention&l;/em&g; on investing than our male counterparts: Women live longer, and so may need more savings to get us to the end of our lives with financial security. Meanwhile, women also tend to have more gaps in their work history (less time to save), and also have average lower pay throughout their careers (less income to save).
It all adds up to a big financial deficit over time, according to new findings in a &l;a href=&q;https://www.ml.com/women-financial-wellness-age-wave.html&q; target=&q;_blank&q;&g;Merrill Lynch/Age Wave study&l;/a&g;. They found most American women face a roughly $1 million gap in lower lifetime pay compared to men. Higher health care costs alone account for an extra $194,000 more in funds needed by women vs. their male counterparts, according to the study. The survey, which queried 3,707 adult respondents last fall (2,638 women and 1,069 men)&a;nbsp;also found most women lacked sufficient investment knowledge &a;mdash; 60%&a;nbsp;reported not having knowledge to invest as their top barrier. And while women were as confident as men in completing financial&a;nbsp;tasks&a;nbsp;such as paying bills (90%) and budgeting (84%), only half (52%) were confident about investing, compared to men (68%).
&l;!–nextpage–&g;
It may be impossible to track down the origins of the lack of confidence. Though&a;nbsp;the report highlights&a;nbsp;examples showing&a;nbsp;a lack of attention to the kinds of specific financial topics&a;nbsp;often affecting women including the&a;nbsp;surprising discovery that there were no widely available financial calculators online that could take into account gaps in employment in a review of 19 calculators from a mix of investment and financial advice sites. Even women&s;s magazines showed a lack of focus on the topic: an analysis of&a;nbsp;1,594 editorial pages in 17&a;nbsp;March 2018 issues of women&a;rsquo;s magazines, also found only five pages, or less than 1%, covered&a;nbsp;financial subjects.
It&a;rsquo;s worth keeping in mind that causation vs. correlation is always tricky, and these are just a couple of studies. What isn&a;rsquo;t at issue, though, are the stakes for getting savings wrong. Most of us lack traditional pensions and must take a greater personal role in managing our investments and savings if we&a;rsquo;re going to have what we need in retirement.&l;/p&g; This entry was posted in Best Stocks on
